entry.title: copyedit 4.1
entry.content:
What I changed and why

I chose to rewrite the beginning of section 4.1, due to it being overly formal and complex.

Before and after

Before One common preprocessing step is to normalize the input text into a standardized form before tokenization. This may involve removing unwanted artifacts, mapping equivalent surface forms to a common representation, or applying lossy simplifications intended to reduce superficial variation in the data. Common surface-level transformations include: ... (good examples) These normalizations are often used to unify minor typographical differences across scripts for easier processing or to clean up erroneous text. Invisible character removal is also important for tokenizer safety, as control characters can be used to inject token breakpoints to alter a model’s output while leaving the surface form of the text unchanged (see also Section 14.3; Boucher et al., 2022).
After Before tokenization, text is often normalised into a standard format, Such that artifacts, escape or control characters do not exist. This is to prevent mapping of two visually similar text to different tokens and consequently different embeddings. ... (examples) Further more, control characters can be used to inject token breakpoints to alter a model’s output. Removing such "invisible characters" helps circumvent that safety risk.

The general rule

Use simple words to convey a simple idea.
entry.summary: One sentence that makes people want to click.

entry.title: One text, many token sequences
entry.content:
The original

Section 2.2 makes the survey’s core point in prose and one equation. A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences, while detokenization is many-to-one, so the probability of a text is the sum over all of its tokenizations,

\[p(s) = \sum_{t \in T(s)} p(t),\]

yet common practice scores only the canonical one. The survey’s overview figure (Figure 1.1) draws tokenization as a single path from raw text to token IDs, so the reader has to assemble the many-to-one picture from the text and the inline “sample sentence” example, against the impression the figure gives.

The redesign

Left: the usual picture, in which text passes through a fixed tokenizer to a single token sequence. Right: the same text spelled three ways, using the example and tokenizations from Section 2.2 (▁ marks a word-initial space). The probability of the text is the sum over all of them, but in common practice only the canonical one is scored.
entry.summary: The survey's core point in one figure: a language model scores token sequences, not text, so the tokenizer is part of the model rather than a preprocessing step.

entry.title: Beyond Fixed Tokenization: New Strategies
entry.content:
This week’s survey discusses several limitations of traditional subword tokenization, including its reliance on fixed vocabularies and segmentation rules that cannot adapt during model training, as well as challenges in generalizing across languages. It also explores alternative approaches, such as byte-level modeling, and highlights the trade-off between sequence length, model performance, and computational cost - emphasizing that fewer tokens do not necessarily mean faster or better models.

The following two papers build on these ideas: the first addresses the computational limitations of byte-level generation, while the second further investigates how tokenization choices affect model efficiency.

1. Fast Byte Latent Transformer (Kallini et al., 2026)

This paper makes byte-level language models faster at generating text by allowing them to predict multiple bytes at once, rather than generating them one by one. The survey discusses Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) as an alternative to traditional subword tokenization, but highlights the computational challenges of byte-level generation. This paper builds on BLT and proposes techniques to make generation more efficient.

2. Compute Optimal Tokenization (Limisiewicz et al., 2026)

This paper investigates how the amount of text represented by each token affects language model efficiency, showing that the optimal degree of token compression (token size) depends on the available computational budget. The survey emphasizes that shorter token sequences do not necessarily mean faster or better models. This paper investigates that trade-off and shows why choosing the right tokenization strategy matters for efficient model training.
entry.summary: Two papers extending the survey's discussion: one addressing the noted limitations of byte-level generation, and the other further exploring the claim of why fewer tokens don't necessarily mean greater efficiency.

entry.title: How language models put words back together

link.title: How language models put words back together

entry.content:
These two papers examine what happens inside the model after tokenization, i.e., how tokens become word representations. Both connect tokenization to specific computations in attention and MLP layers.

Busigin and Pinter (2026) studies how a language model combines word fragments into a representation of the whole word. They feed an already trained model a word as a single token, such as table, and record its internal representation. They then feed the same word split into fragments, such as ta | ble, and compare the representation at the final token with the original. To identify which components contribute to reconstruction, they intervene on attention and MLP outputs, replacing them with activations from other inputs and measuring how the representation changes. They find that attention brings information from earlier parts to the final token, and MLP layers help combine this information into a representation of the full word. Their main contribution is to identify the computations involved in reconstructing words after tokenization.

Kamoda et al. (2025) analyzed how attention selects which word fragments should go together. They studied GPT-2’s learned attention weights, separating contributions from token identities, positions, and their interactions. To study token identity, they fix a token such as iens and calculate its attention score against every token in the vocabulary, independently of any sentence. In one head, sap and Al receive high scores, which corresponds to words such as sapiens and Aliens. They then isolate positional contributions to determine whether the head prefers nearby tokens, and compare these predictions with attention patterns observed in real text. Their main contribution is to show that preferences for compatible subwords and nearby positions can be recovered from the model’s learned parameters.
entry.summary: Understanding how language models reconstruct words from subword tokens.

The original

Table 2.1 of Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP supports a point made in Section 2.2: the vocabulary can account for a large share of a model’s parameter budget, especially in smaller models. The table lists vocabulary sizes, hidden dimensions, parameter counts, and embedding percentages for fifteen models, grouped by family.

The percentage column contains the comparison we need, but the reader has to assemble the picture: scan fifteen rows, mentally rank the percentages, remember the gaps, and look back at model sizes to interpret them. Every entry has the same visual weight, whether it represents almost 60% of a model or less than 1%.

The redesign replaces the table with a graph that makes these differences visible directly.

The redesign

I focus on one question: How much of each model’s parameter budget goes to the embedding and output layers? What the graph makes easier to see

  • Differences are visible at a glance. Bar lengths let readers see how much the parameter shares differ without mentally comparing a column of numbers. Sorting makes the ranking clear and helps both large gaps and small differences stand out.
  • Colors make comparisons easier. Models from the same family share a color, so readers can quickly find related models even when sorting places them apart. This makes it easier to compare models within a family and see how families compare with one another.

Design decisions

  • Sort by percentage. Readers can find the extremes and follow the ranking without constructing it themselves.
  • Focus on one metric. Leaving out hidden dimensions and absolute embedding counts allows the users to focus on what’s important.
  • Preserve family context with color. Consistent colors reconnect related models after sorting.

A smaller share in this graph means fewer parameters allocated to these layers relative to the model’s total; it does not by itself establish better model quality.

Data: Table 2.1, p. 10, shown above.

entry.title: Rewriting Section 3.2 — Unigram Language Modeling Tokenization

link.title: Rewriting Section 3.2 — Unigram Language Modeling Tokenization

entry.content:
What I changed and why

I chose to rewrite Section 3.2, which explains the Unigram tokenization algorithm.

I think the original section gives a good technical overview of the algorithm, but it moves quite quickly through the main ideas. In particular, it introduces the probabilistic model, the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, and vocabulary pruning without really showing how they work together.

For someone who is not already familiar with these concepts, I think it can be difficult to understand the intuition behind the algorithm. For example, it is not immediately clear why we assign probabilities to tokens, how these probabilities are initialized and updated, or how we decide which tokens to remove from the vocabulary.

My goal is to make the explanation more accessible to someone learning about tokenization for the first time. I would first explain the main idea behind Unigram and how it differs from BPE, then go through its training process step by step, using a small numerical example to demonstrate how the probabilities are calculated and updated.

Before and after

Before 3.2 Unigram Language Modeling Tokenization The Unigram tokenization algorithm (Kudo, 2018), sometimes known as UnigramLM or ULM, takes a prob abilistic modeling approach to tokenization. The main underlying assumption of Unigram is that text is the surface realization of samples from a latent-variable generative model. This generative model is parame terized by a unigram distribution; each token in a token sequence is drawn independently from a unigram language model, and the strings we see are the concatenations of them. Tokenization is then simply the recovery of this underlying segmentation. We provide a brief description of the algorithm here; for a more in-depth exposition, see Meister (2025). Given the above probabilistic foundation, the first practical challenge lies in learning the specific parameters— namely, the vocabulary and unigram distribution probabilities. The Unigram algorithm provides a top down vocabulary construction method for learning both of these parameters. The training algorithm uses expectation-maximization (EM) with iterative vocabulary pruning. Starting from a large initial seed vocabulary, the algorithm alternates between: (1) computing expected (E) token counts across all possible segmentations of the corpus, weighted by their probability under the current model; and (2) updating token probabilities via maximum (M) likelihood. After each EM iteration, a pruning step removes tokens whose absence causes the smallest decrease in corpus log-likelihood, continuing until the desired vocabulary size is reached. A reference implementation is given in Code 3.4. At inference time, we must choose a segmentation according to this model. Unigram chooses the most probable segmentation under the model, which can be found efficiently via the Viterbi algorithm (Viterbi, 1967), as shown in Code 3.5. In practice, the Unigram algorithm is primarily defined by its implementation in SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018), which makes several engineering choices not fully specified in the original paper. These include vocabulary initialization via suffix arrays, a Bayesian variant of the M-step, and approximations to the pruning loss computation. Recent work has provided clearer documentation of these implementation details (Land & Pinter, 2026), finding that many expensive defaults have minimal impact on the final tokenizer. MinGram (Land, 2026b) takes this further, replacing the suffix-array initialization with a BPE derived seed vocabulary, marginal EM with hard EM over a minimum-token path, and the iterative pruning loop with a single score-based pruning step. Sequence compression becomes the primary training objective, with the learned unigram score retained only as a tiebreak among equally short segmentations. Unigram provides several advantages over BPE, creating seemingly more morphologically plausible to kens (Bostrom & Durrett, 2020; Vemula et al., 2025b). Despite these advantages, its adoption has been limited, perhaps in part due to the inference efficiency of BPE, which makes it an appealing choice for practitioners. Due to its probabilistic nature, Unigram naturally supports subword regularization (see Sec tions 3.7 and 8): sampling from the distribution over segmentations during training, which can improve model robustness (Kudo, 2018). BPE achieves a similar effect only through ad hoc modifications such as BPE-dropout (Provilkov et al., 2020)
After

The Main Idea

Unigram is a probabilistic tokenization algorithm. Unlike BPE, which starts with individual characters or bytes and gradually merges them into larger tokens, Unigram works in the opposite direction. It starts with a large vocabulary of possible tokens and gradually removes the ones that are less useful.

The main idea is to assume that a word can be constructed by independently sampling tokens from a probability distribution over the vocabulary.

For example, consider the word playing. Depending on the vocabulary, it could be represented as:

  • playing
  • play | ing
  • p | lay | ing

All three tokenizations represent the same word, but Unigram assigns each one a different probability.

If a tokenization consists of the tokens \(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_k\), its probability is defined as:

\[ P(t_1,\ldots,t_k)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(t_i) \]

Here, \(p(t)\) is the probability assigned to token \(t\). These probabilities are learned during training, and their sum over the entire vocabulary must equal 1:

\[ \sum_{t\in V}p(t)=1 \]

The goal of Unigram is to find a vocabulary and token probabilities that assign high likelihood to the training corpus.

Initializing the Vocabulary and Probabilities

Before training begins, we need to construct an initial vocabulary and assign probabilities to its tokens.

Unlike BPE, which begins with a small vocabulary, Unigram starts with a much larger set of candidate tokens.

In the SentencePiece implementation discussed in the paper, the initial vocabulary contains all characters appearing in the training corpus, together with a large number of frequent substrings. These candidate substrings are identified using a suffix array.

For example, if our corpus contains words such as play, playing, and player, the initial vocabulary might contain:

\[ V=\{\text{p},\text{l},\ldots,\text{play}, \text{ing},\text{playing},\text{player},\ldots\} \]

We also need to assign an initial probability to each candidate token. The exact initialization depends on the implementation. SentencePiece uses initial scores for its seed vocabulary.

To understand the idea, one possible initialization is to use the frequency of each candidate token in the training corpus. If \(c_0(t)\) is the number of times the candidate token \(t\) appears in the training corpus, we can define:

\[ p_0(t)=\frac{c_0(t)}{\sum_{u\in V}c_0(u)} \]

Here, the occurrences are counted as substrings, before choosing the final tokenization of the text. This gives more probability to frequently appearing candidates while ensuring that the probabilities sum to 1. This is an illustrative initialization and not necessarily the exact initialization procedure used by SentencePiece.

The important point is that these probabilities are only initial estimates. During training, the EM algorithm updates them according to how well the tokens explain the training corpus.

A Simple Example

Suppose our vocabulary contains the tokens play, ing, and playing, with the following initial probabilities:

Token Probability
play 0.40
ing 0.30
playing 0.10
Other tokens 0.20

These probabilities are chosen only to make the example simple. Now suppose we want to tokenize the word playing.

For simplicity, assume there are only two possible tokenizations.

Option 1: Represent the entire word as one token.

\[ P([\text{playing}])=0.10 \]

Option 2: Split the word into two tokens.

\[ P([\text{play},\text{ing}]) =0.40\cdot0.30=0.12 \]

Since \(0.12>0.10\), the second tokenization has a higher probability according to our model. Therefore, the tokenizer would choose:

\[ [\text{play},\text{ing}] \]

This illustrates how Unigram makes its decisions. Instead of following a predetermined sequence of merges, as BPE does, it compares the probabilities of possible tokenizations and chooses the most probable one.

However, we still need to understand how these token probabilities are learned.

Learning the Token Probabilities

Unigram uses an algorithm called Expectation-Maximization (EM) to learn the token probabilities.

The difficulty is that the training corpus contains words, but we do not know which tokenization should be used for each word. For this reason, EM alternates between two steps.

E-step: Estimating Token Counts

In this step, we consider all possible tokenizations of each word and calculate their probabilities.

Returning to our example, the two possible tokenizations of playing had probabilities \(0.10\) and \(0.12\). The total probability assigned to the word is:

\[ P(\text{playing})=0.10+0.12=0.22 \]

We can now calculate the probability of each tokenization, given that the observed word is playing:

\[ P([\text{playing}]\mid\text{playing}) =\frac{0.10}{0.22}\approx0.455 \]

\[ P([\text{play},\text{ing}]\mid\text{playing}) =\frac{0.12}{0.22}\approx0.545 \]

These probabilities tell us how likely each segmentation is, given the observed word.

Instead of choosing only the most probable segmentation during training, we use both to calculate the expected number of occurrences of each token.

For this example, the expected counts are:

Token Expected Count
playing 0.455
play 0.545
ing 0.545

For example, play appears only in the second segmentation, so its expected count is \(0.545\).

In practice, these expected counts are calculated over the entire training corpus.

M-step: Updating Token Probabilities

After estimating the expected counts, we update the probability of each token by dividing its expected count by the total expected number of tokens.

The update rule is:

\[ p_{\text{new}}(t)= \frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{count}(t)]} {\sum_{u\in V}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{count}(u)]} \]

For our simplified example, the total expected count is:

\[ 0.455+0.545+0.545=1.545 \]

Therefore, the updated probabilities would be approximately:

\[ p_{\text{new}}(\text{playing}) =\frac{0.455}{1.545}\approx0.294 \]

\[ p_{\text{new}}(\text{play}) =\frac{0.545}{1.545}\approx0.353 \]

\[ p_{\text{new}}(\text{ing}) =\frac{0.545}{1.545}\approx0.353 \]

Notice that these probabilities sum to 1, up to rounding. In this simplified corpus, the other candidate tokens have zero expected counts.

Here we considered only one training word to keep the calculation simple. With a real corpus, the update would account for all the words and all their possible segmentations.

The algorithm repeats the E-step and M-step. The updated token probabilities change the probabilities of possible segmentations, which in turn change the expected token counts.

This process improves the likelihood assigned to the training corpus under the current vocabulary.

Removing Tokens from the Vocabulary

So far, we have only learned probabilities for the tokens, but Unigram also needs to decide which tokens should remain in the vocabulary.

As mentioned earlier, the algorithm begins with a large vocabulary containing many possible substrings. However, keeping all these tokens would require a large embedding table in the language model.

To reduce the vocabulary size, Unigram periodically removes tokens. The important point is that we do not simply remove the tokens with the lowest probabilities.

Instead, we estimate how much the likelihood of the training corpus would decrease if a particular token were removed.

Conceptually, we can define the loss caused by removing token \(t\) as:

\[ \operatorname{Loss}(t)= \log P(D\mid V)- \log P(D\mid V\setminus\{t\}) \]

Here:

  • \(D\) is the training corpus.
  • \(V\) is the current vocabulary.
  • \(t\) is the token we are considering removing.
  • \(V\setminus\{t\}\) is the vocabulary after removing token \(t\).

The probabilities also depend on the token probability parameters, which are omitted from the notation for simplicity.

The idea behind this equation is to compare how well the model explains the training corpus before and after removing the token.

A small loss means that the token can be removed without significantly affecting the likelihood assigned to the data.

Example: Removing a Token

Let's return to our previous example, where the training corpus consists only of the word playing.

Recall that the initial probabilities were:

\[ p(\text{play})=0.4,\quad p(\text{ing})=0.3,\quad p(\text{playing})=0.1 \]

For simplicity, assume there are only two possible tokenizations:

\[ [\text{playing}] \qquad\text{and}\qquad [\text{play},\text{ing}] \]

The total probability assigned to the word using the current vocabulary is:

\[ P(D\mid V)=0.1+(0.4\cdot0.3)=0.22 \]

Now suppose we want to remove the token playing from our vocabulary.

After removing it, the only remaining possible tokenization is:

\[ [\text{play},\text{ing}] \]

If we temporarily keep the probabilities of the other tokens unchanged, the remaining score assigned to this word is:

\[ P_{\text{remaining}}(D)=0.4\cdot0.3=0.12 \]

Therefore, the decrease in log-likelihood under these fixed scores is:

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Loss}(\text{playing}) &=\log(0.22)-\log(0.12)\\ &=\log\left(\frac{0.22}{0.12}\right)\\ &\approx0.606 \end{aligned} \]

This shows that removing playing eliminates one possible way to represent the word, but another segmentation remains available.

This calculation is a simplified illustration using fixed scores. After permanently removing a token, the remaining probabilities must be normalized and can later be re-estimated by EM. Therefore, the actual change in corpus likelihood can be different from \(0.606\).

Now imagine a larger corpus containing many occurrences of player, playing, and playful.

Removing play might affect many different words, whereas removing playing might be less harmful because it can be replaced by play and ing.

We would therefore prefer to remove the token with the smaller estimated removal loss.

Tokenization During Inference

Once training is complete, the tokenizer has a fixed vocabulary and a probability assigned to each token.

When a new word is given, the tokenizer needs to find the sequence of vocabulary tokens with the highest probability.

For a tokenization consisting of \(t_1,\ldots,t_k\), this means finding:

\[ z^*= \arg\max_{z\in T(w)} \prod_{t\in z}p(t) \]

Where \(T(w)\) is the set of all valid tokenizations of the input word \(w\).

Equivalently, using log-probabilities:

\[ z^*= \arg\max_{z\in T(w)} \sum_{t\in z}\log p(t) \]

Since a word may have many possible segmentations, enumerating all of them individually can be expensive.

Instead, Unigram uses the Viterbi algorithm, a dynamic programming algorithm that efficiently finds the most probable segmentation by reusing the best solutions for shorter prefixes of the input.

The result is a deterministic tokenization. However, Unigram can also sample different tokenizations according to their probabilities during training, a technique known as subword regularization.

Summary

To summarize, the Unigram algorithm works as follows:

  1. Start with a large vocabulary of candidate tokens and initialize their probabilities.
  2. Use EM to estimate how frequently each token is used and update its probability.
  3. Estimate how much the corpus likelihood would decrease if each token were removed.
  4. Remove the least useful tokens and repeat the process until the desired vocabulary size is reached.
  5. During inference, use Viterbi to find the most probable tokenization of the input.

The general rule

What rule did you apply that others could use in their own writing? (e.g. “Lead with the finding, not the method.”)
entry.summary: a detailed explanation of the unigram tokenization

entry.title: Reimplementing BPE-Dropout
entry.content:
What I reimplemented

I reimplemented BPE-Dropout (Provilkov et al., 2020; Code 3.7 in Section 3.7) and evaluated three empirical properties of stochastic tokenization from Section 8.1.1 (Subword Regularization) across dropout rates p in [0.0, 0.8]:

  1. Typo & Transliteration Robustness (Example 8.1): Measuring how often stochastic segmentations of "intelligence" (vs. typo "intellegence") and my cat’s name, "burekas" (vs. transliteration variant "bourekas"), expose shared subword tokens.
  2. Subword Semantic Drift: Tracking how dropping ('s', 'l') in "manslaughter" allows 'man' to merge with 's' ('mans'), leaving 'l' + 'aughter' to form ('mans', 'laughter').
  3. Quasi-Determinism (Cognetta et al., 2024c): Measuring the probability mass concentrated in the Top-3 most frequent segmentations as p.

The code

import random
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Verified BPE Merge Table (lower index = higher priority)
MERGE_LIST = [
    # --- Example 8.1: "intelligence" vs "intellegence" ---
    ('i', 'n'), ('t', 'e'), ('e', 'n'), ('c', 'e'), ('en', 'ce'),
    ('l', 'l'), ('in', 'te'), ('inte', 'll'), ('i', 'g'),
    ('intell', 'ig'), ('intellig', 'ence'), # Clean (p=0): ('intelligence',)
    # Typo path for "intellegence" -> ('intell', 'eg', 'ence') (no single-char tokens!)
    ('e', 'g'), ('intell', 'eg'),

    # --- Fun Case 1: "manslaughter" -> ('manslaughter',) vs ('mans', 'laughter') ---
    # Build 'man' and 'aughter' first; then ('s','l') competes directly with ('man','s')!
    ('m', 'a'), ('ma', 'n'),
    ('a', 'u'), ('g', 'h'), ('te', 'r'), ('au', 'gh'), ('augh', 'ter'),
    ('s', 'l'),           # Higher priority: 's'+'l' -> 'sl' -> 'slaughter' -> 'manslaughter'
    ('man', 's'),         # Competing merge if ('s','l') is dropped: 'man'+'s' -> 'mans'!
    ('sl', 'aughter'), ('man', 'slaughter'),
    ('l', 'aughter'),     # Now 'l' + 'aughter' merges into 'laughter'!

    # --- Fun Case 2: My cat "burekas" vs "bourekas" ---
    ('b', 'u'), ('r', 'e'), ('k', 'a'), ('ka', 's'),
    ('bu', 're'), ('bure', 'kas'),          # Clean (p=0): ('burekas',)
    ('o', 'u'), ('b', 'ou'), ('re', 'kas')  # Variant (p=0): ('bou', 'rekas')
]
assert len(MERGE_LIST) == len(set(MERGE_LIST)), "Duplicate merge pair!"
RANKS = {pair: i for i, pair in enumerate(MERGE_LIST)}

# 2. Algorithm 3.3 + Code 3.7 (BPE-Dropout)
def bpe_tokenize(word: str, ranks: dict, p: float = 0.0) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    pretoken = list(word)
    while len(pretoken) > 1:
        possible_merges = [
            pair for pair in zip(pretoken, pretoken[1:])
            if pair in ranks and random.random() > p
        ]
        if not possible_merges:
            break
        best_pair = min(possible_merges, key=lambda pair: ranks[pair])
        
        new_pretoken, i = [], 0
        while i < len(pretoken):
            if i < len(pretoken) - 1 and (pretoken[i], pretoken[i + 1]) == best_pair:
                new_pretoken.append(pretoken[i] + pretoken[i + 1])
                i += 2
            else:
                new_pretoken.append(pretoken[i])
                i += 1
        pretoken = new_pretoken
    return tuple(pretoken)

# 3. Console Sanity Check
random.seed(42)
print("Clean (p=0):", bpe_tokenize("intelligence", RANKS, 0.0))
print("Typo  (p=0):", bpe_tokenize("intellegence", RANKS, 0.0))
print("Cat   (p=0):", bpe_tokenize("burekas", RANKS, 0.0), "vs", bpe_tokenize("bourekas", RANKS, 0.0))
print("Crime (p=0):", bpe_tokenize("manslaughter", RANKS, 0.0))
print("Crime samples (p=0.2):", Counter([bpe_tokenize("manslaughter", RANKS, 0.2) for _ in range(200)]).most_common(3))

# 4. Run Monte Carlo Evaluation (N = 2000 per p)
p_vals = np.linspace(0.0, 0.8, 17)
N = 2000

typo_intel = set(bpe_tokenize("intellegence", RANKS, p=0.0))   # {'intell', 'eg', 'ence'}
typo_burekas = set(bpe_tokenize("bourekas", RANKS, p=0.0))     # {'bou', 'rekas'}

intel_overlap, burekas_overlap, top3_mass, laughter_rate = [], [], [], []

for p in p_vals:
    s_intel = [bpe_tokenize("intelligence", RANKS, p) for _ in range(N)]
    s_bur   = [bpe_tokenize("burekas", RANKS, p) for _ in range(N)]
    s_ms    = [bpe_tokenize("manslaughter", RANKS, p) for _ in range(N)]
    
    intel_overlap.append(sum(1 for s in s_intel if set(s) & typo_intel) / N * 100)
    burekas_overlap.append(sum(1 for s in s_bur if set(s) & typo_burekas) / N * 100)
    top3_mass.append(sum(c for _, c in Counter(s_intel).most_common(3)) / N * 100)
    laughter_rate.append(sum(1 for s in s_ms if "laughter" in s) / N * 100)

# 5. Plot Results
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].plot(p_vals, intel_overlap, 'o-', label="'intelligence' vs 'intellegence'")
axes[0].plot(p_vals, burekas_overlap, 's--', label="My cat: 'burekas' vs 'bourekas'")
axes[0].set(title="1. Typo & Variant Overlap (%)", xlabel="Dropout p", ylabel="Shared Subword Rate (%)")
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(p_vals, laughter_rate, '^-', color='#d95f02')
axes[1].set(title="2. 'manslaughter' -> 'laughter' (%)", xlabel="Dropout p", ylabel="Hit Rate (%)")

axes[2].plot(p_vals, top3_mass, 'd-', color='#7570b3')
axes[2].set(title="3. Quasi-Determinism: Top-3 Mass (%)", xlabel="Dropout p", ylabel="Mass in Top-3 (%)")

for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(0.1, color='gray', linestyle=':', label='p=0.1')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Results

All three metrics align with the theoretical claims in Section 8.1.1:

  • Subword overlap on Example 8.1 & "burekas" (Panel 1): At p = 0.0 (deterministic BPE), "intelligence" (('intelligence',)) and "intellegence" (('intelleg', 'ence')) share 0% of their tokens, as do "burekas" (('burekas',)) and "bourekas" (('bou', 'rekas')). At p = 0.1, shared subword overlap jumps to ~30% for "intelligence" (exposing 'ence') and ~8% for "burekas" (exposing 'rekas'), peaking around p = 0.25–0.35 (~70% and ~11%) before dropping near 0% at p = 0.8 as words fracture into individual characters.
  • The "manslaughter" → "laughter" effect (Panel 2): At p = 0.0, "manslaughter" deterministically merges into ('manslaughter',) (0% "laughter"). Under BPE-dropout, ('mans', 'laughter') becomes the second most frequent segmentation, hitting ~8% at p = 0.1 and peaking at ~13.5% at p = 0.20–0.25 before decaying to 0% at high p when 'aughter' itself fails to merge.
  • Quasi-determinism & high-p character collapse (Panel 3): At p = 0.1, ~87% of all segmentations of "intelligence" fall into the Top-3 splits, confirming Cognetta et al. (2024c)’s claim that BPE-dropout samples quasi-deterministically rather than uniformly. Diversity peaks at p = 0.6 (Top-3 mass drops to ~14%), after which Top-3 concentration rises back to ~39% at p = 0.8 because extreme dropout forces runs into the same unmerged character sequence.
  • Why token IDs differ from Example 8.1: Example 8.1 lists GPT-4 (cl100k_base) token IDs. Because production Rust tokenizers (tiktoken) hardcode deterministic merges and do not expose the inner loop for per-step dropout, I used a local priority table over the target words.

What I learned

  • BPE-dropout’s narrow sweet spot (p ≈ 0.1–0.2): Low p remains heavily concentrated on the canonical path, moderate p exposes shared stems for typos and transliterations ("intellegence", "bourekas") at the occasional cost of semantic drift ("laughter"), and high p collapses words into single-character noise—motivating length-biased samplers like GRaMPa (Bauwens et al., 2025).
  • Merge competition mechanics: Because Code 3.7 re-evaluates all valid adjacent pairs at every while iteration, dropping a high-priority merge (('s', 'l')) for a single step only alters the final tokenization if an adjacent lower-priority merge (('man', 's')) immediately consumes one of its boundary tokens.

entry.title: Making the small share of tokenization research visible

link.title: Making the small share of tokenization research visible

entry.content:
The original figure

The paper argues that tokenization receives little research attention compared with other parts of language models. It introduces Figure 2.1 with the following paragraph.

Taken together, these factors have greatly limited experimentation with tokenization relative to other areas of the neural language modeling stack. This disparity is reflected in the number of tokenization-related papers published each year in premier venues, compared to the total number of NLP papers, as shown in Figure 2.1. In 2025, papers about tokenization (though not necessarily exclusively about tokenization) made up at most 2% of all papers.

Cognetta et al. (2026), p. 10. Read the paper

However, the grouped bars draw attention to the increase over time and the differences between venues. The small share of papers discussing tokenization is less visually apparent. We redesigned the figure to make the paper’s main point easier to see, showing these proportions on a full 0–100% scale.

The redesign

What changed and why

  • Each full bar represents all abstracts at that venue. The blue segment makes the small share mentioning tokenization-related terms immediately visible.
  • The bars show 2025, when the share was highest at every venue. Even then, it was only about 2%.
  • Percentages make the proportions easy to interpret. The table gives the values for every venue and year.

The original figure makes changes over time easier to compare. The redesign puts the small share of mentions in focus, matching the point made in the accompanying paragraph.
entry.summary: Redesigning Figure 2.1 to show how few abstracts mention tokenization.

entry.title: 2 papers challenging the tokenization survey
entry.content:
The Survey paper is a substantial body of work covering many questions and issues regarding tokenizers. I looked for two recent papers that deal with, and challenge, assumptions and claims from the survery:

  • Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them (Schaeffer & Koyejo, November 2026): Bits per byte (BPB), an evaulation metric for tokenizers, is defined as “agnostic” to the tokenization process. This paper claims that the BPB metric can favor particular tokenizers and vocabulary sizes even when the language models are untrained. This complicates the survey’s use of BPB for cross-tokenizer comparison, as it is biased in a way and therefore less reliant.

  • Language-Specific Effects of Tokenizer Choice in Multilingual Language Models (Meister, Altıntaş & Bosselut, October 2026): One key challenge that’s addressed in the survey is multi-lingual tokenizations, and cross-lingual tokenization. The central claim is that tokenizers are biased towards lagnuages that are prominent in the dataset, and advocate twoards higher allocation of training resoursces to these low-frequency languages. This paper trys to reallocate more tokenizer training-data to lower-resource language. The result, across 123 models and 54 tokenizers, gives an overall HIGHER PBP. This might mean the PBP metric itself is problematic (as claimed in the paper above), or that, as the autorhs suspect, extra vocabulary entries may receive too little language-model training to learn useful embeddings.
entry.summary: Recent papers question how we evaluate tokenizers and how we help underrepresented languages.
